analysis.one_liner: Gives federal student loan borrowers a bill of rights: capped payments, disclosure rules, fee limits, and bankruptcy relief.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee the day it was introduced in February 2007 and never received a vote or a hearing, dying when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed federal student loan borrowers a set of basic rights: monthly statements showing exactly what they owe and what they have paid, a legal cap on monthly payments tied to their income, limits on the collection fees charged on defaulted loans, expanded loan discharge for borrowers who are medically unable to work, and the ability to wipe out student debt in bankruptcy after seven years. It also would have required colleges that tout graduates' job prospects to publish real employment, earnings, and default data, and would have made colleges that illegally steer students to preferred lenders liable for the borrower's entire loan. It was introduced by Sen. Hillary Clinton with four cosponsors and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and some private student loan borrowers — current students and graduates carrying debt — who would gain affordable income-based monthly payments, clear billing statements, warning notices before default, caps on collection fees and total charges, disability and bankruptcy discharge rights, and a formal appeal process to the Education Department when lenders violate their rights. Borrowers who are victims of colleges' illegal preferred-lender arrangements could recover the full loan amount from the college.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to cap a borrower's total monthly student loan payment based on income — 10% of income between 100% and 200% of the poverty line and 20% of income above that — with no late or underpayment fees if the capped payment is made on time, and with the federal government covering excess interest on subsidized loans.

Amends federal bankruptcy law so that student loan debt, educational overpayments, and obligations to repay scholarships can be discharged in bankruptcy once they have been due for more than seven years, reversing the near-total protection student lenders enjoyed under the 2005 bankruptcy law.

Caps collection fees on defaulted federal loans at 7.5% to 18% of the balance depending on how the loan is resolved, requires itemized expense lists, and directs the Department to cap the total interest and fees that can be charged over 10, 15, and 20 years.
Expands loan discharge for borrowers unable to work because of a serious medical impairment lasting at least 60 months, not only those judged permanently and totally disabled.

Requires lenders to give monthly itemized statements, disclosures before consolidation (including the loss of federal protections if consolidating with private loans), and default warnings; requires colleges that publicize graduates' job prospects to publish real placement, earnings, and default data; and makes colleges liable for the full loan amount if they pay prohibited incentives to admissions officers. It also bars colleges from delaying loan processing for students who use unpreferred lenders.

analysis.who_pays: FFEL student loan lenders, guarantee agencies, and debt collectors would lose collection-fee revenue and the near-absolute bankruptcy protection that made student loans exceptionally safe to hold; the federal government would cover excess interest on subsidized loans for low-income borrowers; colleges — especially those relying on loan volume and optimistic placement claims — would bear new disclosure duties and full-loan liability for steering violations.

drawbacks.text: The income-based payment cap creates real costs for taxpayers: the bill requires the federal government to pay the difference between the interest owed and the capped payment on subsidized loans, and loan balances forgiven or discharged through bankruptcy shift losses to the government and taxpayers.

Restoring bankruptcy discharge for student debt after seven years reduces the collateral security of student loans, which lenders argued would raise borrowing costs or tighten credit for the students lenders are least sure will repay; the 1% fee on subsequent consolidation loans also adds a cost for repeat consolidators.

The disclosure requirement turns on the Secretary of Education designating 'disclosure institutions,' and the caps on total charges are left to the Department to set at unspecified levels — both would depend heavily on how a given administration enforced them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits to borrowers — affordable payments, capped collection fees, discharge rights, and honest placement data from colleges — are substantial for the roughly $54 billion borrowed in a single academic year and would come mainly at the expense of lenders' and collectors' unusually profitable default and collection business. The main honest costs are the federal interest subsidy for low-income capped payments and the standard lender objection that easier bankruptcy discharge makes student lending riskier. On balance the bill shifted risk from borrowers back to lenders and taxpayers in ways most consumer advocates would call a fair trade, though its enforcement mechanisms left much to the Education Department's discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee on February 7, 2007, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Hillary Clinton introduced the Student Borrower Bill of Rights Act of 2007 on February 7, 2007, joined by Sens. Mikulski, Kerry, and Lieberman.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The complete action history shows no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

The bill's findings noted that federal student borrowing had grown 76% in a decade and private student credit had grown 734%, and that income-contingent repayment was unavailable to many borrowers facing unaffordable payments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan lenders, guarantee agencies, and debt collectors, whose collection-fee revenue and near-absolute bankruptcy protection remained untouched, along with colleges that preferred not to publish placement and default data. Borrowers got none of the payment, fee, or bankruptcy relief the bill promised.

for.name: Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sens. Barbara Mikulski, John Kerry, and Joseph Lieberman

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 7, 2007 and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Student loan industry (FFEL lenders, guarantee agencies, and collectors)
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in defeating the bill's collection-fee caps, income-based payment limits, and restored bankruptcy discharge; the industry was actively lobbying against borrower-friendly reforms during the 2007 loan scandal.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats plus one Independent, but the bill never advanced far enough for any recorded vote or stated opposition, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: FFEL student loan lenders and servicers
industries.note: The bill would cap collection fees on defaulted loans at 7.5%–18% and cap borrowers' total interest and fees, cutting directly into the default-collection revenue that made federally guaranteed student loans exceptionally profitable. Income-based payment caps and refinancing rights would also curb fee and interest income.

Defaulted federal loans carried steep collection charges that the bill would cap and require to be itemized and justified against actual expenses. Default is where student loan collection is most lucrative, so the cap targets the industry's core profit channel.

industries.industry: Colleges, especially for-profit and loan-heavy institutions
industries.note: Colleges advertising graduates' job prospects would have to publish real placement, earnings, and default figures, and any college caught paying prohibited incentives to admissions officers would owe the borrower the entire loan amount. Institutions where loans supply most revenue would face the closest scrutiny.

The bill would require lenders to warn borrowers that consolidating federal loans with private loans strips away federal protections, and would direct a study of private-loan rate hikes and fees as potentially exploitative — groundwork for future regulation of a fast-growing market.
